Dhurandhar: The Revenge

✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

NOT A WOKE TRAP. Dhurandhar: The Revenge is aggressively, unapologetically nationalist from its opening frames. There is no bait-and-switch. Jaskirat Singh Rangi's mission, his sacrifices, and his vendetta against the forces behind the 26/11 attacks are the entire movie. Western critics calling it 'propaganda' are essentially confirming the VirtueVigil trad score: this film presents India's intelligence services, its soldiers, and its national grievances as heroic and righteous without qualification. A movie has to earn the word 'propaganda' from people who hate patriotism. Dhurandhar earns it.

Overall Perspective

Dhurandhar: The Revenge is the kind of movie that makes you understand why Bollywood's nationalist wave is not going anywhere. At 229 minutes, Aditya Dhar's sequel to his 2025 spy epic is the eighth-longest Indian film ever made, and it earns almost every minute. This is a movie with genuine ambition: not just to entertain, but to reckon with documented historical events that Indian audiences have lived with for decades. The IC-814 hijacking. The Parliament attack. The 26/11 Mumbai massacre. Dhar names names. He depicts actual operations. He builds a spy hero whose mission is inseparable from those real wounds.

Ranveer Singh plays Hamza Ali Mazari, whose real identity is Jaskirat Singh Rangi, a Punjabi Sikh whose family was destroyed by political violence before he was recruited by Indian intelligence and deployed inside Pakistan's criminal underworld. The film opens with that backstory in full: his father hanged by a local strongman's goons, his sisters assaulted, his elder sister murdered. Jaskirat kills the men responsible, goes to prison, and is then extracted by intelligence officials who see a man with nothing to lose, fluent in the world they need him to penetrate.

This is classic hero origin architecture, and Dhar uses it without irony. By the time we reach the film's contemporary sections, Hamza has become a major figure in Karachi's criminal networks, close to Dawood Ibrahim's organization, navigating rivalries between Baloch and Pathan gangs while covertly advancing India's intelligence interests. The structure is a slow-burn accumulation: relationships built and burned, covers nearly blown, handlers killed, and the creeping horror of a man who has lived as his enemy for so long he has to remember what he's actually fighting for.

Singh is extraordinary in the role. He played Bajirao Mastani with theatrical intensity, and Padmaavat with operatic physical commitment, but Hamza requires something different: stillness, the quiet menace of a man who has survived by disappearing into other identities. Singh gives him depth without softness. When Hamza kills, and he kills a great deal, Singh lets us see what it costs without making it into therapy. The film respects its protagonist's violence as consequential rather than spectacular.

R. Madhavan as Ajay Sanyal, the intelligence official clearly modeled on NSA Ajit Doval, brings the film's institutional side to life. Akshaye Khanna, in the handler role, operates in that cold bureaucratic register he has perfected across decades of Indian cinema. The ensemble is stacked: Sanjay Dutt and Arjun Rampal in supporting roles that serve the story rather than their star value.

Western critics have called it propaganda, and their complaints tell you exactly what the film is. The New York Times said it was 'a movie of the current moment, which isn't exactly a comfort.' Screen-Space complained that the film uses 'a scarred national conscience as a means to justify its hero's sociopathic proclivity for stabbings, burnings, decapitations and countless bullet riddlings with exploitative glee.' JoySauce called it 'problematic.' These are not film criticisms. They are political disagreements with the film's premise: that India has real enemies, that those enemies committed real atrocities, and that the people who fought back deserve to be celebrated.

For VirtueVigil readers: the critics giving it bad reviews are the same critics who gave glowing reviews to films that mocked American military culture. The Indian audience has voted. They turned Dhurandhar: The Revenge into the fourth-highest grossing Indian film of all time. A film that gets banned by Gulf Cooperation Council countries for its content is, by definition, not propaganda serving power. It is a film that power finds threatening.

The criticisms that deserve engagement are the ones about pacing and runtime. At 229 minutes, the film is long in places where it doesn't have to be. The seven-chapter structure gives Dhar room for his historical scope but also room for self-indulgence. Some sequences that should land as gut punches are diffused by their position late in a very long film. Shashwat Sachdev's score is consistently strong, and the cinematography by Vikash Nowlakha gives the film a visual weight appropriate to its subject, but a film this long lives and dies by its editing rhythm, and the editing does not always serve the emotional beats.

Those are craft criticisms, not cultural ones. As a statement about national identity, sacrifice, and the cost of intelligence work, Dhurandhar: The Revenge is the best Bollywood has offered in years. It treats its audience as adults. It does not moralize about violence; it contextualizes it. It does not question whether India's enemies were real; it shows you what those enemies did. And it gives you a hero who paid a price no one asked him to pay, for a country that needed someone willing to pay it.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Aditya Dhar

NATIONALIST/CONSERVATIVE. Dhar is one of the most politically clear-eyed filmmakers working in Indian cinema today. His debut, Uri: The Surgical Strike (2019), was a box office phenomenon that celebrated India's military response to Pakistani-backed terrorism. Dhurandhar and its sequel continue that project on an even grander scale, weaving actual historical events into a spy epic that treats Indian intelligence as the last line of defense against real and documented threats. Dhar does not pretend to be neutral. He makes movies for people who love India and believe its enemies are real.

Aditya Dhar broke through with Uri: The Surgical Strike in 2019, which became one of the highest-grossing Bollywood films of that year and launched the phrase 'How's the josh?' into the national conversation. He spent years developing the Dhurandhar duology, shooting both parts back-to-back. The films represent his most ambitious work yet: a 443-minute total runtime chronicling a RAW operative's decades-long mission inside Pakistan's criminal and political underworld. Dhar wrote, directed, and produced both films. He is the rare Indian filmmaker who combines genuine patriotic commitment with genuine filmmaking craft.

Writer: Aditya Dhar, Ojas Gautam, Shivkumar V. Panicker

Dhar wrote the story and screenplay, with Gautam and Panicker providing additional screenplay work. The script's most impressive achievement is its structural ambition: seven chapters spanning roughly a decade of real Indian history, integrating the IC-814 hijacking, Operation Lyari, the 2014 election, and the 26/11 attacks into a single coherent narrative arc. The dialogue reported by critics as effective includes lines that land because they are grounded in genuine stakes. These are not invented villains. The film names Dawood Ibrahim. That takes confidence.

Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative audiences in the US who responded to Top Gun: Maverick and Sound of Freedom will find a kindred spirit in Dhurandhar: The Revenge, with the important caveat that this is a much harder film than either of those. The violence is graphic and sustained. The moral terrain is darker. Maverick is about proving yourself in the air; The Revenge is about surviving for two decades inside your enemy's infrastructure while watching people you respect die around you. If you are willing to engage with a nearly four-hour Indian spy thriller on those terms, this is one of the most serious and confident pieces of nationalist cinema made anywhere in the last decade. The box office tells you the audience found it. The 987 US theaters and $4.6M opening weekend tell you the Indian diaspora came out for it. This one matters.

Parental Guidance

Not rated; extremely graphic violence comparable to Munich or Zero Dark Thirty. Sexual violence in the origin story is present but handled with gravity rather than exploitation. No sexual content otherwise. Strong language throughout. 229-minute runtime requires adult attention and endurance. Recommended for ages 18 and up. Not appropriate for children or sensitive viewers.
